1. e4 {[from the parent game] The king's pawn, two moves.} e5 {[from the parent game] The same.}
2. Bc4 {[from the parent game] The king's bishop, at his queen's bishop's fourth square.} c6
{[from the parent game] The queen's bishop's pawn, one move. (a)} 3. d4 {[from the parent game]
The queen's pawn, two moves.} exd4 {[from the parent game] The king's pawn takes the pawn. (b)}
4. Qxd4 {[from the parent game] The queen retakes the pawn.} d6 {[from the parent game] The
queen's pawn, one move. (c)} 5. f4 {[from the parent game] The king's bishop's pawn, two moves.}
Be6 {[from the parent game] The queen's bishop, at his king's third square. (d)} 6. Bxe6 {[from
the parent game] The king's bishop takes the bishop.} fxe6 {[from the parent game] The king's
bishop's pawn retakes the bishop.} 7. c4 {The queen's bishop's pawn, two moves.} c5 {The queen's
bishop's pawn, one move. (a) NOTE: This move absolutely decides the game. You must leave him no
more opportunity of pushing his queen's pawn: if you can effect this, his king's bishop must
remain imprisoned; and, besides, your pieces will occupy a great deal more ground than those of
your adversary.} 8. Qd3 {The queen, at her third square.} Nf6 {The king's knight, at his
bishop's third square.} 9. Nc3 {The queen's knight, at his bishop's third square.} Nc6 {The
same.} 10. a3 {The queen's rook's pawn, one move. (b) NOTE: This move is very material, because
he would have attacked your queen with his queen's knight, and thereby got one piece more on his
queen's fourth square, in order to push afterwards his queen's pawn, and by that means disengage
his pieces.} Be7 {The king's bishop, at his king's second square.} 11. Nf3 {The king's knight,
at his bishop's third square.} O-O {The king castles.} 12. g3 {The king's knight's pawn, one
move. (c) NOTE: If you had got out and removed your queen's bishop to his king's third square,
your adversary would have played his king's knight to his fifth square, in order to take your
bishop, and thereby set at liberty his king's bishop. Besides, it is advantageous to preserve,
as much as possible, a bishop of the same colour as that of the adversary. The directions of the
bishops are very dangerous, almost in all cases: and the best way to ward off their attacks, is
to oppose bishops to bishops.} Na5 {The queen's knight, at his rook's fourth square. (d) NOTE:
He plays this knight, in order to exchange him for your bishop.} 13. Be3 {The queen's bishop, at
his king's third square.} Nb3 {The queen's knight, at the adverse queen's knight's third
square.} 14. Rd1 {The queen's rook, at its queen's square.} Ng4 {The king's knight, at the
adverse king's knight's fourth square.} 15. Bg1 {The queen's bishop, at his king's knight's
square. (e) NOTE: None of these moves are attended with any danger to you, because they do not
break your centre; and you may dislodge these same knights whenever you please. This proves,
that real attacks cannot be made, but with the help of several united pieces, and very seldom
with one or two.} a6 {The queen's rook's pawn, one move. (f) NOTE: He makes this move, in order
to hinder your queen's knight from attacking his own queen's pawn.} 16. h3 {The king's rook's
pawn, one move.} Nf6 {The king's knight, at his bishop's third square.} 17. Be3 {The queen's
bishop, at his king's third square.} Nh5 {The king's knight, at his rook's fourth square.} 18.
Ne2 {The queen's knight, at his king's second square.} Na5 {The queen's knight, at his rook's
fourth square. (g) NOTE: Instead of moving this knight, he might have sustained him, by playing
his queen to her knight's third square; but you would then have pushed your king's knight's
pawn.} 19. O-O {The king castles. (h) NOTE: In this situation the white must win, if they
prevent the adverse queen's pawn from advancing, by not being too hasty in pushing the pawns on
the right wing, till that king is ready to sustain them. Niv} *
